Breaking.title: Three children and teacher killed by 16-year-old at Oregon primary school
Breaking.text:
A 16-year-old shot dead three children and a teacher at a primary school in the US state of Oregon before he was killed by a bystander, according to police.

The suspect, who has not been named, forced his way into Silver Rail Elementary School in the city of Bend on Thursday afternoon by shooting at locked doors, police said.

Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz said the teenager was shot dead by a community member who "pursued him into the school and engaged him".

The three children killed were aged five, eight and 11. A seven-year-old and a 54-year-old teacher were taken to a hospital in a critical condition, police said. It is unclear if the attacker had any links to the school.

"We are stunned and heartbroken by this senseless tragedy," Steven Cook, the top administrative official of the local school district, said in a statement.

"No words can adequately express the grief our community is experiencing."

Emergency services responded to reports of an active shooter at Silver Rail Elementary in Bend, Oregon, at 12:59 local time (04:59 BST), Bend Police Department spokeswoman Sheila Miller told reporters.

The first call came from a person who said that an unknown suspect was shooting into their car with a long gun, police say. Photos released from the scene show a red truck with bullet holes.

Minutes later, the local county dispatch received multiple 911 calls reporting that the attacker had entered the school.

Police say he shot at locks on the doors in order to force his way inside.

A bystander saw the shooting begin to unfold, pursued the attacker into the school and shot him dead, police said.

Three minutes later, officers arrived at the scene. They confirmed that the attacker had been killed, and then searched the school.

The victims include three children aged 5, 8 and 11 and one teacher, Krantz said.

A seven-year-old child and a 54-year-old teacher were taken to a local hospital with "critical injuries", he added.

While police said the shooter was a local 16-year-old boy, they declined to add further details pending the ongoing investigation.

Police have not released the identities of any victims, the attacker, nor the bystander who shot him.

Schools throughout the city of Bend have been closed on Friday, with officials saying the community needs time to heal.

Around 450 children attend Silver Rail Elementary School, which has more than 40 adult staff members, police say.

Local media reports suggest the school received new doors in 2022 which can lock classrooms with a flip of a switch.

According to the K-12 School Shooting Database, there were 235 shooting incidents at American schools last year and at least 140 so far this year, including this one.

Breaking.title: Bus hits train stopped on French side of Channel Tunnel, with 19 injured
Breaking.text:
A bus has hit a stationary freight train near the French entrance to the Channel Tunnel, injuring the driver and 18 passengers, French authorities say.

The bus, which was carrying lorry drivers due to take a shuttle rail service, struck the train at the loading platform of the tunnel in Coquelles, near Calais, at 19:27 (18:27 BST) on Thursday.

The bus driver and one passenger were severely injured and evacuated by helicopter. None of the injuries were life threatening, a local official said.

Local sub-prefect Agathe Cury said freight and Eurostar passenger traffic through the tunnel had not been disrupted after a brief stoppage to evacuate injured people. An investigation has begun.

"Two trains were on either side of the platform. One was being loaded by heavy goods vehicles ahead of a cross-Channel journey, and another train that had previously been loaded was departing," Cury said.

"For a reason that currently remains unknown, the minibus collided with the departing train.

"The bus did not overturn, it is still upright – but the shock and the collision caused injuries to the people involved."

The incident involved a minibus transporting workers who were about to board Le Shuttle. All were men of different nationalities, she added.

It is not clear whether any British nationals are among the injured.

Cury said it was "the first time an incident of this type has occurred" on an Eurotunnel loading platform.

The BBC's Evan Davis, who was travelling through the Eurotunnel to Calais at the time of the incident, witnessed blue light vehicles "concentrated on one of the platforms" as he entered France.

"There were plenty of cars queueing up at check-in when I drove past just now, and I saw some cars going through check-in, so despite the collision they weren't being held," he said from the scene.

Photos published by local French newspaper La Voix du Nord, external showed a small bus with damage to its front and side standing alongside a train, among a crowd of emergency workers.

Eurostar has released an update saying: "An incident occurred several kilometers away from the Channel Tunnel.

"This incident does not involved or impact Eurostar trains running from and to London. All of Eurostar trains will run as expected."

Breaking.title: Same-day test helps doctors detect hidden infections in critically ill children
Breaking.text:
A pioneering same-day test has been used to detect hidden and drug-resistant infections among children in intensive care.

Respiratory samples from more than 100 critically ill young patients at London's Great Ormond Street Hospital (GOSH) were sent for what is known as metagenomic testing., external

It can identify bacteria, viruses and fungi from a single sample, which in many cases influences what doctors prescribe.

Metagenomics can detect infections that standard tests miss, meaning better outcomes for some critically ill patients.

In March, 10-year-old Willow Crowther became dangerously ill with pneumonia, which triggered a seizure and multiple cardiac arrests.

Willow, from Kent, was admitted to intensive care at GOSH. Her mum, Stacey Moore, was told she had a 50% chance of survival.

"The consultant said... we should bring our family up to say goodbye to her. This is how critical and in how much danger she was of passing away."

The team at GOSH used metagenomics - a diagnostic test that works by sequencing all genetic material present, in contrast to conventional methods where clinicians need to decide in advance what they're looking for.

The test identified that Willow had a drug-resistant bacterial infection which needed a different antibiotic to the one she had been prescribed.

"The fact that they had a test there available to her was paramount. It saved her life," said Stacey.

"It's a miracle she's here and we're extremely grateful for that," added Willow's dad, Russ.

With the right treatment, Willow was eventually able to recover from her infection, but needed several months in hospital.

She is one of many patients at the children's hospital to benefit from the new type of testing.

During a study in 2024-5 metagenomic testing was used on 122 critically ill children in the paediatric intensive care unit (ICU) at GOSH.

The results have now been published in the Lancet Microbe.

Metagenomic testing analyses all genetic material in a sample and can detect thousands of different pathogens.

By contrast, the most common method of identifying bacteria is by trying to culture them in Petri dishes, a technology that has been used since Victorian times.

Another test, PCR, can identify viruses and some bacteria, but doctors need to specify what they are trying to detect.

Metagenomics testing at GOSH was able to identify around nine in 10 bacteria and viruses and all fungi in samples.

In a quarter of cases, the results influenced prescribing decisions, including starting, stopping or changing an antibiotic.

Dr Sam Ray, consultant in paediatric intensive care medicine at GOSH and co-author of the study said traditional testing required clinicians to make an educated guess about which infection they were looking for.

"The study has helped us to spot infections we would have missed, get children on the right treatment and stop antibiotics when we know they aren't going to work.

"Removing unnecessary treatment is incredibly important for the fight against growing antimicrobial resistance."

Metagenomic testing at GOSH also detected 50 organisms not identified by routine diagnostics, meaning it could play an early warning role against new infections.

Dr Julianne Brown, head of the GOSH Metagenomics Service and co-senior author of the study said the new testing was being gradually rolled out to around 30 intensive care units across the UK treating both adults and children.

"It could be a powerful tool for identifying new infections that pose a pandemic threat," she added.

"In the future, if there was to be a new mystery pathogen that could be a cause of the next pandemic, we would detect that very quickly and put the right measures in place."

The project at GOSH builds on trials at Guy's and St Thomas' NHS Trust which first used metagenomics to test for respiratory infections in adult patients.

Breaking.title: Porn showing choking or incest to be banned from early November, government says
Breaking.text:
Online pornography depicting strangulation or incestuous relationships will be banned from early November, the government has announced.

From 6 November, it will be illegal to possess or publish porn which shows strangulation or suffocation, depicts sexual activity between people who are related or shows adults role-playing as children under 16.

The new rules follow a review into porn regulation in 2025 which found depictions of choking were "rife" on popular porn sites and had helped normalise the act among young people.

Conservative peer Baroness Gabby Bertin, who headed the review, said the news came "not a moment too soon".

She told the Press Association the change in law would "send the unequivocal signal" to companies that host and facilitate porn, and also to wider society, that "extreme and violent content that encourages real-life harm is not acceptable".

Her independent review, commissioned by former Prime Minister Rishi Sunak's government, cited an account of a 14-year-old boy asking a teacher how to choke girls during sex.

It warned that people imitating such behaviour "may face devastating consequences".

Non-fatal strangulation is already an offence if someone does not consent - but its depiction online is currently not illegal.

Amendments to the Crime and Policing Bill, which became law in April, sought to ensure such content would be captured by the legislation and made criminal offences in England and Wales.

Justice minister Alex Davies-Jones said it was not about "criminalising harmless sexual preferences".

But she said "porn can shape what people think a healthy relationship looks like, especially young people". Content which "normalises, or even glorifies" violence against women can "blur the line with what is acceptable in real life", she said.

"If you've got this material, delete it. If you're sharing it, stop," Davies-Jones added.

"It's not as harmless as you may think, and after 6 November, it is criminal."

Breaking.title: Trump calls off livestream of Fort Hood attacker's execution by firing squad
Breaking.text:
US President Donald Trump has called off plans to livestream the execution of former US army psychiatrist Nidal Hasan by firing squad.

Trump had previously said he approved of showing the death of the Fort Hood attacker, while Vice-President JD Vance cast doubt on whether it would happen and said he would not watch it.

Trump's decision to cancel the livestream came after widespread criticism in the US and globally. On Thursday, he said that "many very good and well meaning people would rather not watch him die".

"I think streaming the execution for all to see might have been a strong deterrent for the World to witness how America deals with Terrorists and SCUM like Hasan," Trump said.

"He will die, as scheduled, by firing squad, but this event will not be streamed," the president added in the post on Truth Social.

Hasan fatally shot 13 unarmed US military personnel and injured 32 others at a military base in Texas in 2009. His execution by firing squad will be the first military execution in more than 60 years.

Trump said the families of the victims can still view the execution in person if they wish.

"They deserve to witness JUSTICE!" he said.

After the Pentagon announced last week that it would execute Hasan on 3 December 2026 by firing squad and livestream the event, a cascade of criticism quickly followed from human rights groups and many others. The United Nations called the plans "abhorrent".

While there were more than 2,700 executions across 17 countries last year, only two nations carried them out publicly. According to Amnesty International, 11 public executions were known to have been carried out in Iran in 2025 and another six in Afghanistan.

US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth defended his decision to air Hasan's execution online, saying that "people need to understand that there's serious consequences for these types of things".

But as criticism mounted, Trump appeared to hedge his support, saying on Friday that he "absolutely" approved of the livestream plan, but adding that the Pentagon was still "making a determination" on it.

The president also called Hasan "totally nuts".

"I really don't care how he goes, as long as he goes, and I think that the death penalty is a very worthy way of going for him," he said.

After Trump announced he called it off, a Pentagon spokesman said Hegseth had spoken with the US president beforehand.

"The Secretary supports the President's decision, and they are completely aligned," the spokesman Sean Parnell said.

John Galligan, a lawyer for Hasan working primarily on civil issues, told the BBC that Trump's decision to cancel the livestream of his execution "comes as no surprise".

"It was initially a dumb decision and statement by Hegseth to livestream any execution - and it violated the Army's own regulation," Galligan said.

He said Hasan is paralysed from the chest down, something that Trump "allegedly didn't even know" when he approved the livestream plan.

"The damage has already been done - the Army is now just trying to clean up the mess," Galligan said. "It will permanently remain a stain on our military justice system."

He added that it was not clear if Hasan was aware yet of Trump's "reversal" of the livestream decision.

Hasan opened fire in a crowded medical building where deploying soldiers were awaiting check-ups and vaccines.

Breaking.title: Reform faces questions over candidate vetting after undercover filming
Breaking.text:
Reform UK is facing further questions about its vetting procedures for candidates, after undercover filming broadcast by ITV News, external.

In the film, gathered over the course of a year, an undercover reporter is advised by a local party chairman to delete social media posts supportive of far-right activist Tommy Robinson, before being encouraged to apply to stand to be a councillor for the party.

It also shows a former Reform candidate claiming he failed the party's vetting process twice but was still allowed to stand to be a councillor. Reform denies the individual failed vetting in the first place.

Reform said the party had "improved and prioritised its vetting procedures".

In a statement, Reform said that "from time to time, a handful of individuals who do not share our values will initially make it through vetting" but added: "This is the same for all organisations."

It follows undercover filming broadcast on Wednesday night, which showed some of Reform's councillors and candidates using racist, violent and sexist language.

The party said: "There is no room for racism in Reform UK. We always respect due process of investigations and whilst these are ongoing it would not be appropriate to comment on individual cases."

Reform also accused the ITV investigation of "extreme methods of deception" and using false information to obtain an undercover role in Reform's headquarters.

Two years ago, Reform leader Nigel Farage vowed to vet candidates more "rigorously", after the party dropped a series of candidates following reports they had made offensive or racist comments.

However, the party has continued to face questions over the strength of its vetting processes.

Speaking on Thursday, before the latest filming was broadcast, Farage told BBC Look East his party vetted "to a much higher standard than other parties" but "you can't vet for future comments".

ITV News says one of its undercover reporters was asked if he would consider standing to be a councillor, after spending time leafleting with Reform activists.

He meets with the chairman of a local Reform branch in Chester, Ian Frost, who describes the meeting as "the first stage" of the vetting process.

After the reporter says he has previously posted in support of Robinson on social media, Frost advises him to delete the posts.

"Anything where you've got, things, Tommy Robinson or anything like that, okay, I would delete the account and I'd start again," Frost adds.

Farage has said Robinson would not be allowed to join Reform.

Frost later suggests the undercover reporter could apply to stand for the party, saying: "You might become a councillor. You might then want to go to the MP route. So, social media, yeah. And apply."

Frost told ITV News he thought the reporter was a genuine candidate and gave him the benefit of the doubt.

He added that it was not fair to judge people on a single conversation and he had since left Reform for unrelated reasons.

In another part of the film, a former Reform candidate - Alex Lomas - claims he failed the party's vetting process twice, including for sharing social media posts from Robinson.

However, Lomas says a few days after he failed for the second time he was asked to stand for the party.

"On my second application, I got declined on the Friday, I got an email from them on the Tuesday saying you've passed vetting," he is recorded as saying.

"I said, well, I think you better check with your paperwork, mate, because I've just failed on Friday. Now, you're saying I've passed it, I've not changed anything.

"And then I got a phone call a few days later. Hi, will you stand for Reform UK? I'm like, yeah okay."

He stood for Reform in local elections in Oldham in May but did not win a seat on the council.

The BBC has not been able to contact Lomas and he did not respond to requests for comment from ITV News.

Reform denies Lomas failed vetting in the first place.

ITV's undercover report also shows Farage ruling a controversial mayoral candidate Dr Chris Parry – who said the then Deputy Prime Minister David Lammy should go home to the Caribbean – should be made to apologise, but not stand down.

In a conversation at Reform's headquarters, the party's director of communications Ed Sumner suggests Farage is "protecting" Parry.

In response Farage says: "It's showing a bit of sorrow."

In a separate conversation several weeks earlier, where Farage was not present, Sumner is recorded saying Parry is "clearly a racist" and "needs to go".

After apologising to Lammy in January, Parry was allowed to remain Reform's mayoral candidate in Hampshire and the Solent until he was later suspended in March "pending investigation", following comments about a Jewish voluntary patrol service.

Parry told the BBC there was never an investigation and he has since left the party.

He said: "I would urge people to go back to the original contexts and tweets to see what was said and why. They related to reparations and failures by the police and government.

"They will see I always exercise my right to criticise anyone in power or the public eye, whom I judge to be acting against the interests of the British people."

Labour Party chairwoman Bridget Phillipson said: "These latest shocking and deeply disturbing revelations go right to the top of Reform UK.

"Nigel Farage needs to wake up and realise the buck stops with him. He also must urgently explain why he allegedly stood by a blatant racist instead of kicking him out of his party.

"Time and again Farage has had every opportunity to demonstrate leadership and get Reform's house in order and every single time he has failed."

Breaking.title: London suburban housing project wins top UK architecture award
Breaking.text:
A suburban housing development in south London has won the UK's most prestigious architecture award, with judges praising its sensitive design and integration into the surrounding landscape.

Lion Green Road in Coulsdon, comprising 157 homes across five distinctive 13-sided blocks, was named winner of the 2026 Stirling Prize by the Royal Institute of British Architects (Riba).

Designed by Mary Duggan Architects and built with RUFF Architects, it combines affordable and private housing for Croydon Council.

Replacing a former car park on a challenging, sloping site that varies in height by eight metres, Riba president Chris Williamson praised the design as a "new approach to higher density development" creating "a new connection between the bustling Lion Green Road and a distinctive area of green parkland beyond".

Williamson told the BBC that until he went to study architecture he lived in a council estate in the East Midlands, "and every time I go back there all the council houses have been sold off, they're in private hands.

"Which in a way can be a good thing - we're in a homeowning democracy - but the sad thing is they haven't been replaced.

"Every time I go back - without getting too emotional - I think 'where would we have lived?'

"So to me that's why this particular project was important. I think a lot of people from that sort of background live in terrible accommodaiton - temporary accommodation which isn't safe or secure.

"These houses are fantastic and they're part of a mixed scheme so it's got a fantastic feel to it.

"For me it was a very inspirational, emotional, part of the process."

Duggan, who was brought up in south-west London, said the scheme "challenged conventional suburban housing layouts centred on roads, private gardens and clearly defined front and back spaces".

Winding paths and planting weave between the blocks, connecting them and linking shared outdoor spaces.

She said she wanted it to be a public space people felt they could belong to.

"Housing needs to be progressive. People who live in the building have access to green space, allotments."

The site fronts onto Lion Green Road, with low-rise green belt housing set on higher ground to the south and traditional suburban streets to the north.

Breaking.title: CJP, Abhijeet Dipke: India's 'cockroach' protesters set to return despite police crackdown
Breaking.text:
Thousands of 'cockroach' protesters are set to return to the streets of Delhi on Friday, days after police prevented their last mass demonstration and two of their leaders were jailed.

The Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), a youth-led movement seeking electoral reforms, has called on supporters to gather at Central Park in Connaught Place, a busy commercial district.

The call follows the jailing of two CJP leaders for five days after they entered Jantar Mantar, a protest site recently declared off-limits by police.

What began as a campaign against alleged electoral fraud has since become a wider fight over the right to protest. Central Park is not an approved protest venue either.

The Delhi High Court on Thursday declined to pass an order restraining the CJP after a local trader filed a petition citing disruptions to traffic and business as reasons why Friday's protest should not be allowed.

CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke, meanwhile, has named the protest Lehra Do Tiranga, or Wave the Tricolour, as many Indians informally refer to the country's orange-white-green flag as Tiranga. Dipke has said he is prepared to risk arrest himself.

Getting to Central Park, however, may prove difficult. Police barricades and mass detentions prevented many protesters from joining their demonstration last Saturday. Dipke has urged those unable to make it to Delhi to raise the Indian flag and protest wherever they are.

The CJP has come a long way from May, when the movement began with an insult. After India's chief justice likened some unemployed young people to cockroaches, Dipke embraced the label and turned it into an online protest movement.

By July, he and his supporters were filling the streets over examination paper leaks, in protests that forced India's education minister Dharmendra Pradhan to resign. Within months, the "cockroaches" had become one of the most visible expressions of youth anger at Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government.

Now they are taking on something bigger - India's elections.

At issue is a sweeping revision of electoral rolls, known as Special Intensive Revision (SIR), that critics say has removed more than 130 million names, putting legitimate voters at risk of losing their right to vote.

The CJP wants Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar to resign, accusing the poll panel of favouring Modi's ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP). Both the commission and the government deny the allegations.

Friday's march comes less than a week after police prevented the movement's last mass demonstration from taking place, detaining its leaders and deploying officers across the capital before protesters could assemble.

Dipke and two senior organisers, Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka, were detained from within the aircraft upon landing in Delhi.

The capital was put under a sweeping security lockdown. Tens of thousands of police and paramilitary personnel had fanned out across Delhi, sealing roads, shutting metro stations and intercepting protesters long before they could reach Jantar Mantar, where the CJP had planned its mass demonstration.

The BBC witnessed dozens of people being detained, including journalists and students. In footage from across Delhi, protesters could be seen shouting as police seized them by the arms, dragged them across the pavement and pushed them into waiting buses. Some struggled against the officers; others, already detained, pressed towards the bus windows, waving Indian flags.

Those who managed to gather elsewhere were swiftly dispersed. There were also reports of protesters being assaulted by police.

The BBC captured footage, external of a policeman slapping a detained protester inside a bus. The Delhi police did not respond to questions about the use of violence against protesters.

The scale of the crackdown drew accusations that the authorities were determined to prevent the protest rather than police it. The CJP likened the police action to India's Emergency, when civil liberties were suspended between 1975 and 1977.

Delhi police defended the measures as necessary to maintain public order and prevent unauthorised gatherings.

Dipke, Das and Ranka were released on Sunday after agreeing to maintain peace and good behaviour.

Police then took Jantar Mantar off Delhi's list of approved protest sites, telling demonstrators to go instead to Ramlila Maidan, Burari Ground or CBD Ground.

But Jantar Mantar is no ordinary patch of ground. Built in the 18th Century to study the stars, the observatory sits near parliament and has long been one of India's most recognisable stages for public dissent.

The CJP accuses the authorities of pushing protesters away from the seat of power to make their demonstrations less visible and easier to ignore.

On Tuesday, Das and Ranka returned anyway, bringing a handful of supporters. They unfurled the Indian flag and shouted slogans against Kumar. Police said they had entered the restricted site without permission, some by climbing over a locked gate, and violated the conditions of their earlier release.

The following day, Das and Ranka were sent to Tihar Jail for five days in judicial custody. Another organiser, Ajinkya Shinde, was released on a bond to maintain peace and good behaviour.

With two of its key organisers behind bars, the CJP heads into Friday's protest with its leadership depleted, though Dipke insists the march will go ahead and he does not intend to back down.

"I also may be jailed after this, but I am not worried. Tricolour is my pride and I will raise it," he said in a video message.

Police, meanwhile, are preparing for another large gathering in the heart of Delhi.

Senior officers met on Thursday to discuss security arrangements and possible traffic restrictions around Connaught Place, where a demonstration could disrupt one of the capital's busiest commercial districts.

The CJP's campaign is unfolding alongside a separate wave of protests by India's opposition parties, which have also accused the Election Commission of manipulating voter rolls to benefit the BJP.

Last week, opposition leader Rahul Gandhi and other lawmakers attempted to march to the commission's headquarters in Delhi but were stopped by police and detained. Opposition politicians have since taken their grievances to President Droupadi Murmu and marched towards the Supreme Court.

Among those at Monday's march was Neha Bora, a feisty leader of the left-wing All India Students' Association (AISA), who has emerged as another prominent face of the demonstrations.

Detained while leading protesters last Saturday, she was later seen marching with Gandhi and his sister Priyanka Gandhi Vadra.

Although the CJP, student organisations and opposition parties have largely protested separately, their demands have increasingly converged. Gandhi has condemned the arrests of CJP organisers and called for Jantar Mantar to be reopened to peaceful demonstrators.

Home minister Amit Shah, meanwhile, has accused opposition parties of spreading falsehoods about the voter-verification exercise and defended the Election Commission's independence.

Breaking.title: Trans people should use hospital spaces according to biological sex, NHS England says
Breaking.text:
Trans patients should be cared for on single-sex hospital wards or bays that align with their biological sex rather than their gender identity, according to new NHS England (NHSE) guidance.

It says when this is not "clinically appropriate" then alternative arrangements should be made and the dignity and safety of all patients should be maintained.

The guidance also says staff facilities should be used by people based on their biological sex, while trusts should ensure enough alternatives to single-sex facilities, such as single-occupancy toilets, are offered.

Previous NHSE guidance suggested patients and staff could be accommodated on wards or use facilities based on their gender identity.

That meant that a trans woman – a biological male who identifies as a woman – could have chosen to be on a women's ward, or a trans man – a biological female who identifies as a man – could have opted for a men's ward.

That guidance was withdrawn following the Supreme Court ruling in April 2025 that under equality law the term "sex" means biological sex and "woman" refers to a biological woman.

The judgment said for a space or service to be single sex it should only allow those of the same biological sex to use it.

Also under the new guidance issued on Thursday, NHSE emphasised that in order to avoid discriminating against trans people they should be offered gender neutral spaces.

But the guidance also says decisions may have to be made on a case-by-case basis and must ensure clinical needs are met.

It also makes clear that there are circumstances where clinical need is the overriding priority, including on emergency units and urgent care settings.

In addition to the patient document of the guidance, NHSE has published advice for trusts on how to organise changing rooms, toilets and other single-sex facilities for staff.

Again, it says they should be used by people based on their biological sex, not their gender identity.

The document encourages NHS trusts in England to carry out an audit to ensure they are offering enough alternatives to single-sex facilities, for instance, gender neutral or single occupancy toilets.

Pressures on hospitals mean many have already struggled to keep wards single sex.

NHSE data shows that the number of breaches of the previous mixed-sex accommodation guidance has been growing every year since 2021- where members of the opposite sex were placed on a single-sex ward.

The most recent figure for August 2026 shows there were 5,520 breaches, compared to 3,853 in June 2025.

Sex-based rights charity Sex Matters has welcomed the guidance as a "momentous shift back to reality", but is concerned about how it will be applied.

"NHS patient data is a mess, with potentially thousands of trans-identifying people recorded as the opposite sex," CEO Maya Forstater said.

Trans rights organisations TransActual and Trans+ Solidarity Alliance have said they are concerned NHS staff will be unclear on how to safely look after trans patients.

"This guidance will not survive contact with reality in resource-strapped hospitals and will create unworkable operational challenges," they said.

The NHS has been at the centre of a number of high-profile arguments over the interpretation of equality law and workplace regulations.

In January 2026, Darlington Memorial Hospital was found to have violated the dignity of a group of nurses who complained about a transgender colleague - a biological male who identified as a woman - being allowed to use the female changing rooms. The nurses were told they should change somewhere else if they objected.

The tribunal concluded that the trust had indirectly discriminated against them.

The nurses are currently seeking £400,000 from the NHS to cover their legal costs.

One of the nurses who brought the action, Bethany Hutchison, who is now president of the Darlington Nurses Union, says they welcome the "clear and necessary guidance" from NHSE, but the test will be whether trusts follow it.

"The Darlington nurses should never have had to take their own employer to court to secure privacy, dignity and lawful single-sex facilities," she said.

"Enforcement cannot continue to depend on the courage and personal sacrifice of individual nurses."

In Scotland, another employment tribunal found, in December 2025, that a nurse, Sandie Peggie, had been harassed by NHS Fife over its interpretation of rules on single sex spaces.

Peggie had complained about a doctor, who was a trans woman, using the female changing rooms.

She was suspended after raising concerns. The tribunal dismissed her other claims of discrimination and victimisation.

Breaking.title: Jeffrey Donaldson: Former DUP leader sentenced to 15 years for child sex abuse convictions
Breaking.text:
Jeffrey Donaldson has been sentenced to 15 years in prison for a series of child sex offences, including one count of rape.

The former DUP leader stood with his hands clasped in front of him in the dock of Newry Crown Court as his sentence was handed down.

Judge Paul Ramsey said Donaldson's crimes, which took place between 1985 and 2008, had led to a "catastrophic descent into disgrace".

He was sentenced to 11 years for his crimes against Victim B and four years for offences against Victim A.

The 63-year-old, who was convicted in June, is seeking to appeal his convictions.

Both sentences will run consecutively.

But Donaldson will spend only half his 15-year sentence behind bars.

Because the offences were committed before the Criminal Justice (Northern Ireland) Order 2008 came into effect, he qualifies for 50% remission.

Should his attempt to appeal his convictions fail, it means he will be released from prison at the end of 2033.

The remainder of his sentence will be under supervision in the community on licence.

Donaldson will also be required to sign the Sex Offenders Register for life.

The former Lagan Valley MP has been in Maghaberry Prison since then and returned to it on Thursday afternoon after being sentenced.

Donaldson spends up to 18 hours a day in his cell at the prison, which holds around 1,600 inmates.

Since being convicted, he has been held in its Moyola Unit, a part of the jail used for prisoners with health care needs, and does not share a cell.

It is thought he is in this unit for his own safety from risk of attack or verbal abuse from other prisoners.

Judge Ramsey said aggravating features include the length and protracted nature of the offending spanning many years.

He also took into account the youth of the victims and the age difference between them and Donaldson, adding that he could not accept Donaldson's lack of other convictions as a mitigating factor.

The judge said by contesting a case, a defendant avoids the reduction in sentence they would have got if they had pleaded guilty.

"It is highly significant that the defendant denied the offences to the police, he denied them in evidence and to the probation officer he continues to maintain his denials," the judge said.

"He has doubled-down in his denials.

"There has not been, and doubtless will not be, one word of regret, apology or shame from this man to at least provide his victims with some crumb of comfort."

Jeffrey Donaldson's wife, Eleanor Donaldson, had faced a trial of the facts on mental health grounds, meaning the jury was asked to find out if she did the acts or did not do the acts of which she was accused.

The jury found that she had done the acts in relation to five charges – including four counts of aiding and abetting her husband's offending.

She has applied to appeal the verdict.

She cannot be given a prison sentence but could be given a treatment order or an absolute discharge.

The judge is due to decide on this at a later date.

Statements from both victims were released after the sentencing and read out by Det Ch Insp Leah Crothers.

Victim A said the impact of the crimes committed against her did not end when the abuse ended.

"For years I carried shame, anger and guilt, and questioned whether I was worth protecting or worthy of being loved.

"The last few years have been nothing short of a battle.

"The conviction does not erase the abuse or undo the impact of what happened to me, and I will always carry the consequences of it.

"But those responsible do not control me now. They forever changed me, but they will not take my future. The cycle is being broken and it ends with me."

Victim B said what happened to her as a child had "affected everything since then".

"What would it be like not to be afraid at night, not to wake up shaking, not to have nightmares and not to lock away every feeling I have?

"What happened took away my ability to trust people and, in all honesty, I don't think I really know what trust or love truly is. Nothing can ever change what was done to me. I wish it could.

"I stood up, many years later, because for me this is about drawing a line in the sand and knowing that the Donaldsons can no longer hurt anyone else.

"Many people get to look ahead and plan their lives with hope, I've never known what that feels like. My hope was taken away from me a long time ago."

Jeffrey Donaldson's time in politics began in 1985 when he was elected for the UUP as an MLA in South Down.

In 1997, Donaldson became the MP for Lagan Valley, representing the UUP. He would remain an MP until 2024.

However, in 2003, he quit the UUP and defected to the DUP.

Donaldson was awarded a knighthood in the 2016 Queen's Birthday Honours list, and, in 2021, Donaldson became leader of the DUP.

He remained leader until March 2024, when he was charged with sexual offences of a historical nature.

He was found guilty of all 18 child sex abuse charges, including one count of rape, in June 2026.

Donaldson subsequently asked for his knighthood to be forfeited and tendered his resignation from the Privy Council with immediate effect.

In July, Donaldson was stripped of his knighthood by the King.

Breaking.title: Russia accuses Ukraine of attacking oil refinery after Zelensky says strikes to resume
Breaking.text:
Russia has accused Ukraine of attacking an oil refinery on Thursday after President Volodymyr Zelensky said such strikes, halted at the request of the US, would resume.

Zelensky said he had restricted attacks for three days while Russia continued striking Ukraine's energy infrastructure. "We're done," he told the Financial Times, external.

Russian President Vladimir Putin said Kyiv had also tried to hit refineries on Wednesday - which Ukraine denied - but there had been no "significant damage".

Zelensky also accused the US of withdrawing intelligence-sharing to pressure Kyiv into ending attacks but Ukrainian defence sources later told the BBC some functionality on Starlink satellite services had resumed.

They said "operation while on the move", part of Starlink's military service Starshield, had been restored, although it remains unclear whether restrictions on the speed at which drones could fly while still maintaining Starlink internet connection have been fully lifted.

Officials were still working to clarify "the reasons and circumstances" behind the move, the sources added.

In a separate development, seven people are missing after a drone attack set a chemical tanker on fire off Romania, according to naval officials. Moscow said it had hit two cargo ships with military cargo heading to Ukraine's Odesa port, without naming them.

The Kremlin said Kyiv had "attempted a large-scale attack" on a refinery south of Moscow early on Thursday.

According to Russia's defence ministry, four missiles and dozens of drones were intercepted and the falling debris caused a fire at the site in Ryazan.

Zelensky said dozens of Ukrainian cities had come under Russian attack in the past day.

He previously said he would agree to the "energy ceasefire" announced by US President Donald Trump on Sunday if Moscow also abided by it.

But he accused Russia of ignoring the proposed deal within hours of it being announced, with strikes leaving hundreds of thousands of Ukrainians without power. The Kremlin never said it had agreed to the deal.

Zelensky agreed that he felt betrayed by the US when asked by Piers Morgan on Wednesday night, after Washington appeared to withdraw key elements of its support.

European leaders have rallied around the Ukrainian president. Italy's Defence Minister Guido Crosetto told the BBC that the US restricting its intelligence-sharing with Kyiv would be a "complete mistake".

"Because it is a fundamental form of support. This means denying a country any chance of defending itself."

He added: "Peace will be achieved when Putin will be convinced that there is a stalemate... that he cannot advance anymore. But if he sees a weakness on the Ukrainian front, if the United States takes its resources away, then Putin will think he can win, and so he will continue the war."

Zelensky met Nato chief Mark Rutte as a two-day summit of European leaders began in Brussels on Thursday. The head of the military alliance said they had discussed "the importance of implementing an energy ceasefire as well as Nato allies' continuous support for Ukraine".

Zelensky told the FT that Ukrainian officials had been told by US counterparts that "if you will not stop [the strikes], we will block intelligence".

Ukraine's military relies on US early-warning alerts of incoming Russian aerial attacks to mount air defences, limiting successful strikes, while Starlink internet links are used throughout its war effort to guide drones and protect its skies.

There were suggestions a technical glitch was to blame for the sudden Starlink restrictions on Tuesday evening, but owner Elon Musk appeared to deny this and suggested it was the Trump administration's doing.

"It was not a technical problem, it was the will," Zelensky told the FT.

Trump has denied halting intelligence-sharing. Starlink's sister service Starshield is provided to Ukraine under a US defence department contract. The BBC has approached the US authorities for comment.

That deal was the latest effort by Trump to lower fuel prices in the US ahead of the midterm elections, after months spent grappling with the political consequences of the Iran war, which has sent fuel costs skyrocketing.

Zelensky told the FT: "The question will be: when will the next deal be? Maybe it will be gas. Definitely it will be gas."

With Russia continuing to strike Ukraine, Zelensky suggested the disruptions to US support was no coincidence.

Local officials report at least 13 people were killed across Ukraine on Wednesday in what Zelensky called a "constant", large-scale Russian attack. He said more than 850 drones had been launched at dozens of cities and communities.

At least three people were killed in the central region of Kirovohrad as it suffered its largest attack since Russia's full-scale invasion began in 2022, officials there said, with nearly 360 drones launched during a 10-hour barrage. Deaths were also reported in Donetsk, Kherson and Volyn.

"It is clear that Russia deliberately escalated these attacks, taking advantage of the easing of sanctions and seeing attempts to pressure Ukraine," Zelensky wrote on social media.

Business.title: Banks say Healey is planning Budget tax raid on their profits
Business.text:
Senior banking executives have told the BBC they expect the sector to be "on the menu" when the chancellor announces his Budget in two weeks' time.

John Healey has described the banks as part of "the crown jewels" of the UK economy, yet has refused to rule out a raid on the sector.

The biggest four banks collectively made around £15bn profit in the first six months of this year, leading to calls from trade unions and others for additional taxes.

However, the banking sector trade body, UK Finance, warned that "further increases in bank taxes would weaken competitiveness, discourage investment and job creation, and work against the government's ambition to deliver growth in every postcode".

The UK's biggest banks and building societies currently pay a surcharge of 3% on top of the baseline 25% rate of corporation tax, plus a levy on the assets held on their balance sheets.

The sector contributed nearly £40bn to the Treasury last year, if income tax on employees is factored in.

The bank levy generated £1.4bn last year and the surcharge a further £1.2bn.

There are a number of ways the chancellor could extract more money from the sector.

The 3% surcharge was reduced from 8% under Rishi Sunak, at the same time as he raised corporation tax from 19% to 25%. Returning the surcharge to its previous level could raise around £2bn a year.

The bank levy currently charges 0.1% on outstanding short-term loans and 0.05% on longer-dated loans, although mortgages are excluded from the calculation.

In the past banks have successfully argued that higher taxes would risk making the UK uncompetitive with other jurisdictions and would reduce their ability to lend, and therefore be anti-growth.

In truth, banks were pleasantly surprised they were not hit at the last Budget, given the large profits they have been making in recent years. Rising interest rates have expanded the margin between the rate at which they lend to customers and the rate they pay savers.

There is another option that has been discussed with Treasury officials. Currently banks can use losses from the past to offset against profits - thereby reducing their tax bill in any given year. Lloyds in particular has been a beneficiary of this policy, as large losses from the financial crisis have been used to lower tax bills ever since.

Some analysts and bank executives have pushed the idea of a moratorium on this practice for a few years, which would yield an estimated extra £1bn per year for the Treasury. That would provide a windfall while being "a lot more bearable", in the words of one bank executive.

It would also spare foreign banks from an additional hit, including JP Morgan, whose chief executive Jamie Dimon has warned that the UK already has one of the highest tax burdens on banks in the world. He warned that adding further sector-specific taxes could discourage investment and damage competitiveness.

However, industry leaders say any form of tax rise that hits UK banks and exempts foreign banks' operations in the UK would be hard to square with the government's push to back British business.

Whatever form it takes, banks believe the chancellor now has much more of an appetite to take a larger slice of their pie.

Business.title: I find it quite demoralising in store - why I do all my shopping online
Business.text:
Jess Bacon does all her clothes shopping online.

As a plus-size woman, she finds the size ranges available in stores unreliable. "The sizing in store is notoriously bad. I find it quite demoralising in store," she says.

"The average size woman in the UK is a size 14 or a size 16. I think a lot of people just don't feel seen or represented," says the 29-year-old from Peterborough.

Jess, a culture journalist and author, finds shopping online "much quicker than going into a store, paying for parking, trying things on".

And she feels posting back items that don't fit is less hassle than returning in store, while frequent visits to her local post office give her "more of a community connection".

Jess notes Primark is one of the few High Street retailers where plus-size people can shop. In her experience, Primark stores usually stock up to a size 22.

But soon she'll have the option of staying home even for this - as, after years of holding out, Primark now plans to launch a home delivery service in Britain.

Even throughout the Covid-19 pandemic, when shops were closed, Primark didn't offer the ability to shop online. In 2022 it launched a click-and-collect service, but shoppers still had to travel for their purchases.

The retailer has not said when it expects to launch the service, but has bought a warehouse in Sheffield to enable it to ship products to homes.

Analysts say the decision shows Primark is facing major challenges from ultra-fast-fashion brands such as Shein.

Business.title: 'I paid thousands to a company for healthcare jobs that didn't materialise'
Business.text:
A company has been accused of promising jobs in the healthcare sector which never materialised, leaving people thousands of pounds out of pocket.

Registered in 2025, Synetal Solutions Ltd says it offers career-focused training programmes in the healthcare and IT sectors.

But the BBC has spoken to a number of people who claim they were promised training and support to secure sponsored healthcare jobs that never became available to apply for.

London Citizens Advice says it has seen an increase in recruitment-related scams since the government stopped overseas recruitment for care workers, external. The charity described the firm's practices as "unethical".

Synetal Solutions says it "takes these concerns seriously and disputes the broad allegation that its services or candidate outcomes are fictitious".

Apurv Patel, who has been in the UK on a Skilled Worker visa since 2023, said he paid Synetal Solutions £3,600 across February and March for healthcare training after he and a friend were verbally promised guaranteed sponsored jobs.

Eight months later he has received no job offers, interviews or meaningful employment support, he said.

"I'm frustrated. I paid money, I wasted my time. I did whatever they wanted without any result," he said.

"It's had a miserable effect on my family and finances."

Patel said he did receive some training but described it as poor quality and ultimately "worthless".

Having previously worked for two years as a healthcare assistant, he said he became concerned when a trainer was unable to answer routine questions about care work.

"She didn't give us any answers and we realised she didn't have any experience of healthcare," he said.

The company disputes claims that training was ineffective.

He also alleged communication with the company deteriorated after he made his second payment, with responses sometimes taking several days.

Patel has since complained to his bank and sought help from Citizens Advice.

The BBC has seen emails from the company advertising a "three-month recruitment programme" offering "training and placement with sponsorship" for £5,500.

Home Office guidance, external states agencies may charge for services such as training or CV-writing assistance, but cannot charge fees solely for finding, or attempting to find, employment.

Responding to questions about its marketing, Synetal Solutions said: "We acknowledge the 'guarantee' wording in the emails supplied and recognise that contractual terms alone do not resolve concerns about those assurances."

As part of its programme, Synetal Solutions created accounts for trainees on iHasco, a health and social care training platform.

The BBC contacted iHasco, which confirmed the company was a customer. However, it said its terms did not permit customers to resell its training content to individuals who were not employees.

The company said it was reviewing Synetal Solutions' account and would take appropriate action if necessary.

Synetal Solutions said it had acted in accordance with its agreement with iHasco.

The Care Quality Commission said there was no single qualification that automatically qualified someone to work as a care worker. Instead, providers are responsible for ensuring employees are appropriately trained and competent for their roles.

The BBC also contacted a number of healthcare organisations whose logos appeared on Synetal Solutions' website as examples of employers where graduates had worked.

Those organisations that responded said they had no links to the company. Some also said they had not authorised the use of their branding, and some said they would not accept certificates provided through the company's training.

Daniel Blake, director of London Citizens Advice, described the company's approach as "exploitative".

"The promises that were made are impossible promises," he said. "They are targeting people with vulnerable immigration status.

"This company is asking for large sums of money upfront without any reputable standards, without any reputable evidence of success, and yet when it goes wrong they are refusing to take any responsibility.

"For us, it seems a very unethical way of conducting business."

He added that no reputable recruitment agency would guarantee a successful outcome without first assessing a candidate and matching them to a suitable role, and urged anybody asked to pay large sums upfront to seek independent advice.

"If it seems too good to be true, it probably is," he said.

The company's website stated: "Synetal Solutions provides the right support, guidance, and guaranteed job placement to help you succeed."

But since the BBC contacted Synetal Solutions mentions of job guarantees were removed from the website.

Its social media channels also promoted healthcare as "one of the most reliable paths" for people seeking visa-sponsored work in the UK.

Sarah and Rahul, whose names we have changed, said they paid £3,000 to Synetal Solutions while seeking sponsored employment before the expiry of their student visas.

Rahul, a former dentist in India, could remain in the UK on a graduate visa for longer, but Sarah's immigration status was close to expiring.

To pay the fee, the couple said they borrowed money from a family friend and took out a loan.

Rahul said he was shocked by the quality of the training.

"The mentor didn't know anything about healthcare," he said.

The couple said they were also shown the names of established healthcare providers, including Bupa, as examples of potential employers. Bupa told the BBC it had no connection with the company.

Synetal Solutions says some of their candidates "told us they had secured employment with Bupa" and the reference was "not intended to suggest a formal partnership with Bupa".

It says it had not verified those outcomes and "cannot attribute the recruitment decisions to our training".

Rahul said he secured one or two interviews, but prospective employers rejected the certificates he had received through the programme.

The couple said Synetal Solutions had since stopped responding to their messages.

"We're desperate," Sarah said. "We don't see any other way out."

Blake told the BBC: "If it seems good to be true, it probably is. If you are considering handing over money upfront then seek advice."

He said that "if people have given money and haven't received the service that they were entitled to they should seek redress".

"First of all, make a complaint directly to the company, then to Trading Standards.

"If people feel a criminal offence has happened, we would encourage and support them to go to the police."

A government spokesperson said: "We know how much distress scammers cause to their victims, which is why we will do everything in our power to protect hardworking families and vulnerable customers.

"Our reforms have provided Companies House with new and improved powers to prevent companies from acting unlawfully and to query, remove and share suspicious information."

Synetal Solutions said: "We provide training and employment assistance and maintain supporting records. Recruitment, sponsorship and visa decisions depend on employers and the Home Office."

The company said it had records of genuine candidates who had secured jobs and sponsorship through its services.

Business.title: How data centres became the sleeper issue that could decide the US midterms
Business.text:
A year ago, a longtime US senator was not thinking much about data centres. ​​

Now, according to one of his advisers, he is having regular meetings with staff to track their impact and working on new legislation aimed at curbing their rapid expansion across the country.

"This happens sometimes, something starts slow and then it goes fast," the senior policy adviser to the Democratic senator told the BBC. The person spoke on condition of anonymity as they are not permitted to speak to the press.

The 180-degree turn in this senator's attention was driven almost entirely by a growing wave of public backlash that has seen politicians across the country scramble to keep up. Public sentiment has turned against the expansion of data centres, the large warehouses that store processing power needed for internet activity.

Packed with rows and rows of computer chips, sometimes seven-feet high, data centres have turned into more than infrastructure for the internet. They are now the physical embodiment of the recent and explosive growth of artificial intelligence (AI) technology, and the varied fears people associate with it.

"I don't want to be the guinea pig for this," Indiana resident Angelita Soriano told the BBC.

A new Amazon data centre is being built directly across the street from her home. When complete, the 26-building structure will take up more than a square mile in her neighbourhood and maintain 782 diesel-powered generators.

Some data centres are even larger. In Ohio, a joint effort between OpenAI, Nvidia, SB Energy and the US Department of Energy is set to build a data centre complex that will stretch for roughly six square miles, the same size as most townships in the US.

There are about 3,000 data centres currently operating in the US, with that number potentially doubling in the next few years, according to a report by, external Pew Research Center.

Data centres are built through very local rules and permits, meaning federal lawmakers like US senators have little say in the process.

Yet, opposition has become so strong so quickly in the US that suddenly, politicians at all levels are now all but required to take a stand.

"This isn't just an issue on the left, there is huge pushback among conservatives to data centres," Chloe Autio, an AI policy adviser, said. "Whoever articulates a clear position and sticks to it, in either party, really stands to benefit."

Her analysis was echoed by the adviser to the US senator working on data centre legislation.

"There is a clear policy need here that we're looking to fill," he said. "This is a major backlash across the country - constituents are seeing the impacts of data centres and they do not like them."

That has put many on Capitol Hill - even Republicans - in direct conflict with President Donald Trump, who has championed the unrestrained growth of AI technology.

Trump has dubbed the backlash to data centres a "sick conspiracy" and said people and towns working to keep the buildings out are "backwards and poor".

His ire has been used as a boon to Democratic politicians looking to draw midterm votes from unhappy or undecided constituents.

The BBC spoke to residents of Indiana, Arizona, Michigan, Pennsylvania and Oregon, all of whom have been organising locally against the development of data centres. They expressed concerns about many aspects of the buildings, including their size, construction and operational noise, their impact on air, water and energy resources, as well as the speed at which they seem to be approved by local authorities.

During the first few months of this year, community groups organising against data centres more than doubled to 833, cropping up in almost every US state, according to research from Data Center Watch. The firm collects data for AI industry stakeholders and is part of an AI startup 10a Labs.

Stephanie Maldonado, the political director of LUCHA, a community organising group based in Arizona, referred to the pushback against data centres as "a David and Goliath story" that began several years ago.

"People have been ready to put a stop to it," Maldonado added. "Now, people are angry."

New national polling, external shows that AI regulation and data centres are among some of the top issues for voters this election cycle, behind the ongoing Iran war and various aspects of the economy.

Proponents of building data centres often argue the projects will create more, and better paying, local jobs.

Yet, recent research, external from the Brookings Institution, a non-partisan policy research group, found that a new data centre creates between 100 and 200 local jobs, which is "fewer than industry advocates claim". The projects also have essentially no impact on local wages.

Arizona Governor Katie Hobbs was one such proponent - until public pressure pushed her to the other side of the issue. In July, she enacted a three-year pause on any new tax break given to a company for a data centre project.

Arizona is far from the only state to see politicians react to data centre backlash.

Abdul El Sayed, a Democrat running for Senate in Michigan, made new rules and regulations for data centres a clear part of his successful primary campaign for Senate.

In the race for governor of Georgia, a Democrat who is calling for a pause on data centre development is in a dead heat with a Republican who disagrees.

Republican Senator John Husted of Ohio, who is fighting to keep his seat against Democrat Sherrod Brown, has also had to shift his position. Recent polls, external have found that the majority of Ohio voters oppose data centres. He has softened his support, saying that their arrival should be up to local citizens and elected officials.

Meanwhile, Brown has stumped on his opposition to new data centres. He leads Husted in recent polls.

Husted's trouble in Ohio led the National Republican Senatorial Committee, the major fundraising arm for conservatives in the Senate, to write in a private memo, external that Republican politicians needed to entirely reframe how they spoke to voters on data centres.

"This has become a sleeper issue for the entire election cycle," the NRSC added.

Texas is perhaps the most clear cut example of how backlash has turned into an undeniable issue for even the most pro-business politician.

The state currently has almost 300 operational data centres, with another 170 planned for development, according to Pew data.

At the end of last year, Republican Governor Greg Abbott had boasted of Texas as "the epicentre of AI development" because of the number of data centres it housed.

Within months he was backtracking, citing concerns of "safety and quality of life".

It could play a part in the state's upcoming Senate race too.

Democrat James Talarico's campaign is pushing for an end to "sweetheart tax deals" for Big Tech. He's now seen as a frontrunner for the historically Republican seat, where he is facing off against Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton.

Paxton said in a late September interview that there was still "plenty of open space in Texas that we can put data centres".

Many of the actions or proposals that have come from politicians looking to appease or address these voters are temporary. Most of the moratoriums, for instance, will end in one to three years.

It is possible that the political winds will have shifted by the time such moratoriums expire, leaving Big Tech and AI firms to build as they wish.

For now, people's feelings toward them are strong.

Balaji Tammabattula, the chief executive of Barupon, is developing a roughly 700-acre data centre and technology campus in Liberty, Texas. Despite the buildings being designed to use rain capture for water and supply its own energy needs, an increasingly common design for major data centre projects, Tammabattula told the BBC that people in the community oppose the project out of hand.

"There's just such a high level of tension from the jump that you can't really even break through with the facts," he said.

During a recent community event, Tammabattula said he tried to speak one-on-one with a woman who was vociferously opposed to the project.

"She just looked right at me and said, 'Get the hell out of my state.'"

Business.title: Healey says surprise UK growth is 'sign of resilience' ahead of Budget
Business.text:
The UK economy's stronger than expected performance in August has been called a "sign of resilience" by Chancellor John Healey.

Healey told the BBC "it's really tough in the face of these economic global shocks" as the latest official figures showed the economy grew by 0.1% for the month, defying analysts' forecasts of a slight contraction.

It follows an upgrade to this year's forecast for the UK economy from global watchdog the International Monetary Fund (IMF) earlier this week.

Mr Healey said he wanted "to give people a bit of breathing space from the cost of living and cost of business pressures", promising to do so when he delivers his first Budget in two weeks' time.

Healey did not elaborate on what measures he will take in the Budget, but promised "where we can take action, we will".

But, vowing to keep up the government's approach to fiscal discipline, Healey said "where we want to do things we have to make sure we can pay for them within the Budget that we've got and control spending".

The latest figures from the Office for National Statistics showed the economy grew by 0.7% in the three months to August.

"It's a sign of resilience in the UK economy that some had not expected," Healey said.

The chancellor said the growth was "part of the discipline the IMF here in Bangkok this week has endorsed that they see in Britain".

Britain's economy was boosted in August by an increase in production, which includes manufacturing, oil and gas extraction and energy supply.

The services industry, which makes up the largest chunk of the UK's economy, was flat during the month, while the construction sector contracted.

Over the three months to August, the UK's economy grew by 0.7% overall. ONS director of economic statistics Liz McKeown said computer programming had been the biggest contributor to what she described as "robust" growth over the period.

But she said the production and construction sectors shrank over the three-month period.

August's surprise expansion follows growth of 0.4% in July. The ONS also upgraded its estimate for June's monthly growth to 0.4% from 0.3%.

Paul Dales, chief UK economist at Capital Economics, said Britain's economy was "more robust than we thought".

He warned that an expected increase in inflation would still "dampen growth", but added that the economy was showing "remarkable resilience to higher energy prices and borrowing costs".

PwC senior economist Jake Finney said the development of AI infrastructure was underpinning Britain's relatively strong performance.

"The UK still lags the US in both the scale of that investment and the boost it provides to growth, but it is making progress and remains ahead of many of its European peers," he added.

Healey told the BBC the "impact of AI on the economy, on productivity, is only just beginning to register".

He said the technology has "huge potential, as well as huge risks", adding that Britain's priority would be to ensure AI can be developed safely while unlocking the opportunities it presents.

The latest growth figures were released after Healey landed in Bangkok for the annual meeting of the International Monetary Fund (IMF).

Earlier this week, the global financial watchdog praised the UK's plans to cut debt levels, with global borrowing costs on the rise, with managing director Kristalina Georgieva adding that the country was seeing "a bit of a better growth prospect" than other G7 nations.

Healey said: "Despite conflicts in the Middle East and Europe hitting people across the world, today's figures offer more proof of Britain's resilience in the face of these global shocks."

The Conservatives said the economic growth figures "conceal worrying trends in key sectors as we approach a crucial Budget".

Shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith said: "Construction has now shrunk for four months in a row, with private housebuilding falling fastest. Labour promised to get Britain building, but they are failing."

He called for Healey to cut taxes and reduce red tape.

Liberal Democrat Treasury spokesperson, Daisy Cooper, said the growth of 0.1% in August was "nothing to celebrate".

"The economy is stuck in first gear and barely crawling forward, while families are still struggling to make ends meet."

Healey went on to say the Budget would be tough and not include inflation top-ups for public sector pay.

Some experts and unions have called for extra cash for some departmental budgets, to account for the rising costs of providing public services and pay.

But, asked whether there would be extra money made available for nurses and doctors, the chancellor said: "People recognise these times that are tough for everyone, and what they do expect of a government is to manage with the budgets we've got, deliver the public services they need, and that's the challenge.

"Our departments have their spending, and the prime minister and I, being in lockstep about this, where we want to do things, we have to make sure that we can pay for them within the budgets that we've got and control spending."

Business.title: How much is the minimum wage?
Business.text:
The official minimum rates of pay rose for 2.7 million workers on 1 April.

The rate for workers aged 21 and over is called the National Living Wage, while those aged 18 to 20 are paid the National Minimum Wage.

The rates apply across the UK.

From 1 April 2026, workers over 21 on the National Living Wage are paid £12.71 an hour, 50p more than in 2025.

For someone working full time (37.5 hours a week), that amounts to £24,784.50 a year - an increase of £900.

The rate for 18 to 20-year-olds has gone up to £10.85 an hour.

That's an increase of 85p per hour.

It amounts to an increase of £1,500 a year for a full-time worker.

The government said its goal is to eventually scrap this separate rate for 18 to 20-year-olds, and have one rate for all adults.

The minimum wage for 16 and 17-year-olds has also risen to £8 an hour.

There are different rates of pay for apprentices, external depending on their age and what stage of apprenticeship they are in.

Apprentices aged 16 to 18 are entitled to the National Minimum Wage rate for that age group which is currently £8.

Those aged 19, or in the first year of their apprenticeship, are paid the same amount.

But those over 19 - or who have already completed their first year - are entitled to the appropriate National Minimum Wage or National Living Wage rate for their age.

Some workers do not qualify for either the National Minimum Wage or the National Living Wage.

This includes the self-employed, company directors, volunteers, members of the armed forces and prisoners.

People with disabilities or in long-term unemployment who take part in government work programmes are paid fixed amounts at different stages of the scheme.

These are less than the equivalent National Minimum or Living rate.

Yes. It is a criminal offence for employers not to pay the correct National Minimum and Living Wages to eligible employees.

The rates apply even if workers are not paid by the hour.

If you think you are being paid the wrong amount, you can complain via the HMRC website, external.

You can also get advice from workplace experts Acas, external.

Business.title: Airport drop-off charges to be reviewed after sharp increase
Business.text:
Airport drop-off charges are to be reviewed by the government following sharp price increases in recent years.

Prices at major UK airports have risen by a third since the summer of 2025 on average, according to one analysis, with Gatwick and Stansted drop-off charges found to be the most expensive, jumping from £7 to £10.

Such charges at Edinburgh Airport have risen from £6 to £8.50, while fees at Bournemouth increased from £5 to £8, the same price as Leeds Bradford and London City.

The Department for Transport confirmed it had committed to a review, saying it was "vital to ensure travel remains accessible and that passengers are treated fairly".

The government added it hoped airports would "exercise restraint on rises, particularly where there are limited public transport alternatives".

The RAC, which conducted the analysis in July this year, has campaigned against increases in drop-off charges. It said a review of "kiss and fly" fees would be "music to the ears to drivers".

"We know airport drop-off charges are a growing source of anger and frustration," said Rod Dennis, senior policy officer at the RAC.

"Four-in-five drivers we've surveyed believe they are a 'rip-off', with just one-in-10 understanding why airports charge what they do."

The RAC's research found London City Airport, which only introduced charges in 2026, was the most expensive on a per-minute basis.

Its £8 charge for five minutes works out at £1.60 per minute. Belfast International Airport now charges £5 for 10 minutes in the drop-off zone, up £2 on last year.

None of the top 10 airports in the European Union charge for drop-offs, according to the RAC.

It argues that international airports should not charge for dropping off passengers, however, the industry said the charges were a neccesary part of the business model of airports.

Business.title: Key US voters say economy is getting worse ahead of midterms, exclusive poll finds
Business.text:
With the midterm elections less than three weeks away, key voting groups including independents, rural voters and even some Republicans are increasingly disenchanted with Donald Trump’s economy, according to an exclusive Harris poll for the Guardian.

The majority of those surveyed were pessimistic about the economy, with three-quarters of Americans saying they are concerned about a recession while 61% wrongly believe that the US is already experiencing one. By its typical definition, the US is not currently experiencing a recession.

The poll shows growing weariness across the political spectrum over high prices.

Republicans, fighting to keep control of Congress, are losing support with independent voters, who are expected to be the deciding factor in key swing races. Nearly two-thirds (65%) of independents said the economy was worse, up from 48% who said the same in September 2024 in the heat of the 2024 presidential election.

Even within the Republican ranks, optimism has waned. In February 2025, just a few weeks after Trump was inaugurated, 39% of Republicans said the economy was getting better. By February 2026, just before the US launched attacks against Iran, that optimism was up to 49%. In the latest poll, just 28% of Republicans said the economy was getting better.

Voters say the high prices they are seeing at gas stations and grocery stores will be a key factor when they cast their votes in November. Two-thirds of those polled said that gas prices and grocery prices are their most important issues heading into the election, followed by living expenses, healthcare costs and foreign affairs.

Recent inflation data showed that annualized prices increased 3.7% in September, the highest reading before a midterm election, excluding the pandemic, since 1990.

Energy prices have been especially high since the Iran war, with average gas prices at the pump crossing $1.20 more per gallon compared with a year ago. California drivers, who are experiencing the highest gas prices, are paying on average $6.20 per gallon, according to AAA.

Democrats in swing races have spent much of the last few months framing their midterm battles as a fight, in part, against a growing affordability crisis. James Talarico, the Democratic candidate in a closely watched US Senate race in Texas, has a campaign ad of him holding a paper bag of groceries. “Too many Texans feel like they’re drowning, the cost of groceries, gas, healthcare,” he says in the video.

“They say I can’t win because of my name,” Abdul El-Sayed, another Democratic candidate for a US Senate race in Michigan, said at a recent campaign event. “My name is not the reason your gas prices are through the roof. My name is not the reason you can’t afford your groceries.”

In the new poll, a vast majority of Americans agreed that there was an affordability crisis, including 96% of Republicans. But Americans still remain divided over who has a solution.

Democrats (71%) were more likely than Republicans (59%) to say that their own party had a solution.

Republicans were more likely (26%) to say neither party had a solution compared with Democrats (17%)

Half of independents said neither party had a solution, while 14% sided with Democrats and 10% with Republicans.

Rural Americans, considered a core base for Trump, were more likely to believe that neither party has a solution (41%) compared with their suburban (35%) and urban (27%) counterparts. Four out of 10 of rural Americans said they were living in “survival mode”, where one surprise bill could sink them, compared with 35% of urban and 27% of suburban Americans.

When asked what is most affecting today’s gas prices, 46% of rural Americans said the US government compared with 28% of Republicans who said the same. Republicans were the least likely of any group to blame the US government, instead spreading the blame across oil companies, the Iranian government and natural economic fluctuations.

This survey was conducted online within the US by The Harris Poll from 24 September to 3 October 2026 among a nationally representative sample of 3,998 US adults.
